extractedText: KAIST Develops AI That Reads Brain Waves to Correct Its Own ErrorsKAIST Develops "Neural Value Alignment" Technology AI Reads Brain Waves to Detect User Intent Automatically A Shift From Command-Based AI to Cue-Based AIFinance|Published 2026.09.13. 09:50:25|By Cho Yun-jinjo@sedaily.com|Summary|SaveAAAThe concept of Neural Value Alignment. Photo courtesy of the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)Researchers have developed an artificial intelligence system that corrects its own behavior without being told to do so. The system reads a user's brain waves and adjusts its actions in real time when they diverge from what the user intended.The Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) said on the 12th that Lee Sang-wan, head of its Center for Neuroscience-inspired AI and a distinguished professor in the Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences, developed the technology, called neural value alignment (NVA), in an international collaboration with Microsoft Research Asia. NVA is a next-generation brain-computer interface (BCI) technology that uses human brain waves to align AI with human goals in real time.For AI to collaborate naturally with people, it must accurately grasp what they actually want, the research team said. If a person reaches for a cup, for example, the system needs to determine whether the goal is to drink water or to hand the cup to someone else. Until now, users had to issue new commands or manually correct the machine whenever AI misread the intent behind an action.Photo courtesy of the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)To address the problem, the team focused on prediction errors that arise unconsciously in the brain when a person encounters a situation that differs from what they expected. The researchers examined how the brain responds at the moment a person senses that AI has done something wrong — the instant a thought such as "that's not it" occurs. According to the team, these responses fall broadly into two categories: reward prediction error (RPE), which appears when AI has misunderstood the person's ultimate goal, and state prediction error (SPE), which appears when the goal is correct but the process or method differs from what was expected.The team then applied deep learning to develop a technique that distinguishes how a person is receiving AI's behavior using brain waves alone. The result allows AI to recognize that either the goal or the approach is wrong without the person having to say "that's wrong." The researchers also proposed an algorithm they call neural value alignment-based human-AI synergy, which relays those decoded brain signals to AI in real time so that it can correct its own behavior.In simulations, AI adapted to changes in human intent faster than existing methods under uncertain conditions, such as when a person's goal shifted abruptly or some signals were missing.A KAIST official said the core of the study was demonstrating that AI can read a person's unconscious brain responses and correct its own behavior without being repeatedly told "do it this way" or "that's not right." The official added that as the technology advances, it could be used to help physical AI robots in homes and industrial settings grasp user intent more naturally and adjust their behavior accordingly.Lee said the work is significant because it moves beyond the conventional approach, in which AI inferred human intent solely from observable behavioral outcomes, and shows that cognitive brain signals generated behind those actions can be used directly in collaboration with AI.#KAIST#BrainComputerInterface#NeuralValueAlignment#AI#Neuroscience#DeepLearningOriginal reporting by Cho Yun-jin for Seoul Economic Daily.AI-translated from Korean.
